overview: Ute communities have deep ties to mountain and basin homelands across present-day Colorado and Utah. The map’s large outlines approximate a broad cultural region with many local communities, rather than one state ruled from a capital. The imported starting dates are map coverage markers. Ute history continues through distinct present-day tribes and their relationships to these lands.

periods.title: Mountain homelands and changing connections
periods.summary: Families moved with seasonal resources, while trade and encounters with outsiders changed regional life.

periods.title: Reservations and further land cessions
periods.summary: An 1868 treaty defined a reservation; the 1873 agreement relinquished part while retaining specified rights.

periods.title: Forced relocation and divided lands
periods.summary: White River and Uncompahgre Utes were removed to Utah; southern communities faced smaller land bases.

periods.title: Living tribes and cultural work
periods.summary: Three Ute tribes continue, with their own governments, cultural institutions and teaching programs.

items.text: In western Colorado, family groups moved among different elevations and food sources through the year. Winter brought people into lower, sheltered country. Those routes linked hunting, gathering and visits, requiring detailed knowledge of plants, water and mountain passes rather than wandering without a plan.

The Southern Ute history describes winter evenings spent exchanging stories, repairing tools and making clothing. Relatives camped near one another in sheltered areas. The quieter season was still full of work, but it also gave people time to pass along memories and prepare for future journeys.

Yucca supplied both useful fibers and a root used for soap, according to the Tribe’s household history. Willow and sumac became baskets, and pitch helped make containers watertight. A clean-up material and a water carrier could both begin as plants, then depend on skilled processing.

Wickiups were lightweight wooden shelters whose remains can be difficult to recognize. Archaeologists studying Colorado sites have recorded more than roof poles: their finds include low platforms, a storage shelf and poles built into shelters for practical use. Even an easily dismantled home could have carefully arranged working space.

A 2005-2006 investigation documented 81 wooden structures and other features across twelve sites. Some sites held just one structure; another had 43 features. This variety helps archaeologists investigate small camps and larger gatherings, although a wooden shelter’s shape alone cannot identify every builder’s community.

Tiny moccasins in History Colorado’s collection were probably made for a doll. That interpretation came from representatives of the three Ute tribes reviewing the objects in 2015. The record links them to a family that lived in Dragon, Utah, in the early twentieth century. Children’s play deserves a place in history too.

Around 1830, Antoine Robidoux established a trading post near present-day Delta, Colorado. Trade brought new goods and relationships, but later mining, ranching and settlement placed growing pressure on Ute country. Government agencies increasingly tried to confine people whose livelihoods depended on moving across the landscape.

The Brunot Agreement was negotiated at Los Pinos in September 1873 and ratified in April 1874. It ceded part of the reservation while stating that Ute people could continue hunting there under specified conditions. Other provisions promised annual payments and reaffirmed protections on land that had not been ceded.

In 1881, the United States removed White River and Uncompahgre Utes from Colorado to Utah, including the Uncompahgre under military force. Southern bands were confined to a smaller reservation area. This was a profound dispossession; it did not mean that all Ute people left Colorado or that Ute identity ended.

sections.title: Celebration, children and a living language

items.text: The Bear Dance brings communities together in the spring. A 2015 Southern Ute account explains that its local timing shifted to Memorial Day weekend so young people could attend after school ended. Clothing workshops help participants make shawls, dresses and ribbon shirts. Community tradition includes organizing around children’s lives.

The dance’s final day includes a communal feast. Organizer Tara Vigil described learning from her aunt how much food to order and how to prepare it; the report describes meat-and-vegetable stew cooked in a large pot. Knowing how to feed a crowd is a skill that travels through families.

The Southern Ute Tribal Academy opened in August 2000 with a curriculum that included Ute language. The Ute Mountain Ute program also describes language learning for young children and adults, alongside classes in beadwork, cradleboards and moccasins. Education can connect spoken words with things families make and use.

“Kaan akagar.” means “This house is red.” The online Ute Mountain Ute Dictionary prints the sentence in its grammar guide, whose introduction identifies Southern Ute grammar. This is an attested modern teaching example, linked from the Tribe’s language program, with its supplied English translation.

Today the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Southern Ute Indian Tribe and Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation are distinct tribal communities. Shared Ute relationships coexist with different governments and histories. Ute Mountain’s tribal park also protects Ancestral Pueblo sites, preserving places with more than one people’s history.

ending.text: The imported map cutoffs do not mark an ending. Land seizures and removals profoundly changed Ute life, while three Ute tribes continue to govern, teach and maintain relationships with their homelands.
